title: Long-Term Debt
description: Account for bonds and notes payable, premiums, discounts, interest expense, extinguishments and debt presentation.
html:
Long-Term Debt

Long-term debt includes obligations that are not classified as current liabilities. For FAR, major topics include bonds payable, notes payable, premiums and discounts, interest expense, effective-interest amortization, debt issuance costs, and extinguishment of debt.

1. Bonds Payable

Bonds are debt instruments through which an issuer borrows money from investors and agrees to make specified interest and principal payments.

  • Face value is the principal amount stated on the bond.
  • The stated or coupon rate determines the contractual cash interest payments.
  • The market or effective rate reflects the return demanded by investors when the bonds are issued.
  • The maturity date is when the principal is due.

2. Cash Interest

Cash Interest Paid = Face Value × Stated Interest Rate × Time

Example

$500,000 bonds have a stated annual rate of 6% and pay interest annually.

$500,000 × 6% = $30,000 annual cash interest

3. Bonds Issued at Par

When the stated interest rate equals the market interest rate at issuance, bonds generally sell at face value, or par.

Stated Rate = Market Rate → Bond Issued at Par

4. Bonds Issued at a Discount

If the stated rate is lower than the market rate, investors generally will not pay full face value. The bonds therefore sell at a discount.

Stated Rate < Market Rate → Discount

A bond discount causes the initial carrying amount of the debt to be less than its face value.

5. Bonds Issued at a Premium

If the stated rate is higher than the market rate, investors are generally willing to pay more than face value. The bonds therefore sell at a premium.

Stated Rate > Market Rate → Premium

A bond premium causes the initial carrying amount of the debt to exceed its face value.

6. Effective-Interest Method

Under the effective-interest method, interest expense is based on the bond's carrying amount and the effective market interest rate.

Interest Expense = Beginning Carrying Amount × Effective Interest Rate × Time

7. Discount Amortization

For bonds issued at a discount, effective-interest expense is greater than the contractual cash interest payment.

Discount Amortization = Interest Expense − Cash Interest Paid

Amortizing the discount increases the bond's carrying amount toward face value as maturity approaches.

Discount Example

Beginning carrying amount: $470,000

Effective annual rate: 8%

Annual cash interest: $30,000

Interest Expense: $470,000 × 8% = $37,600

Discount Amortization: $37,600 − $30,000 = $7,600

Ending Carrying Amount: $470,000 + $7,600 = $477,600

8. Premium Amortization

For bonds issued at a premium, contractual cash interest exceeds effective-interest expense.

Premium Amortization = Cash Interest Paid − Interest Expense

Amortizing the premium decreases the carrying amount toward face value as maturity approaches.

9. Notes Payable

Long-term notes payable are generally measured using present-value concepts when appropriate. Interest expense reflects the effective interest rate on the obligation.

If a note is issued at an amount different from its face value, the resulting discount or premium is recognized over the life of the note.

10. Debt Issuance Costs

Under U.S. GAAP, debt issuance costs related to a recognized debt liability are generally presented as a direct deduction from the carrying amount of that debt liability.

These costs are generally amortized to interest expense over the term of the debt.

11. Extinguishment of Debt

When debt is extinguished, the company compares the reacquisition price with the net carrying amount of the debt.

Gain or Loss = Net Carrying Amount of Debt − Reacquisition Price
  • Reacquisition price below carrying amount generally creates a gain.
  • Reacquisition price above carrying amount generally creates a loss.

Extinguishment Example

Net carrying amount of debt: $410,000

Reacquisition price: $425,000

$410,000 − $425,000 = $15,000 loss

12. CPA Exam Focus

  • Compare the stated rate with the market rate to identify par, discount, or premium.
  • Calculate contractual cash interest using the stated rate.
  • Calculate effective interest expense using carrying amount and the market rate.
  • Discount amortization increases carrying amount.
  • Premium amortization decreases carrying amount.
  • At maturity, carrying amount approaches face value.
  • Know how to calculate a gain or loss when debt is extinguished.

quiz.prompt: A bond with a face value of $500,000 and a stated annual interest rate of 6% is issued when the market rate is 8%. How should the bond generally be issued?

choices.text: At face value plus accrued interest

quiz.explanation: Because the bond's 6% stated rate is below the 8% market rate, its contractual interest payments are less attractive than the market requires. Investors therefore pay less than face value, causing the bond to be issued at a discount.
